topic: This is a cross-architecture generalization check for a paper currently built entirely on the Pythia model family. The paper structure is already fixed (do not redesign it) and its three headline claims are: (A) a linear probe from a single early hidden state predicts the sentence embedding of the full eventual continuation, beating weak baselines (mean-embedding, random-match, lexical TF-IDF) and top-k logit-lens token-identity baselines, but losing to a short greedy-rollout baseline (embedding the models own next few generated tokens) at short target horizons; (B) causal semantic steering (probe-derived direction vs random-direction control, alpha tuned relative to the models own hidden-state norm) produces a clearly positive effect (95 percent CI excludes zero); (C) the best layer for passive semantic probing is not necessarily the best layer for causal steering -- this was discovered on Pythia-1.0b, where the passive-best layer gave near-zero steering but a different, earlier layer gave a strong effect. The reuse directories contain the reusable pipeline code and methodology for all of this (baseline/control/rollout comparison, norm-relative alpha tuning, multi-seed steering evaluation with CIs, and the layer-sweep-for-steering approach used to resolve claim C). Your task: replicate claims A and B (not the full six-experiment arc, just these two core comparisons) on ONE Qwen BASE (non-instruct/non-chat) model at a parameter count comparable to Pythia-1.4b (roughly 1-2B parameters, e.g. a Qwen3 base checkpoint of that size) -- confirm you are using a base model, not an instruction-tuned one, since the paper is about raw next-token-prediction dynamics. Use the same 600-prompt set and same sentence-embedding target methodology (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) for direct comparability. For claim B, apply the layer lesson from claim C: do not just use the layer that is best for passive probing -- do a small steering-specific layer scan (at least 4 candidate layers spanning early/mid/late in the network) with norm-relative alpha and multi-seed (aim for 4-5 seeds) evaluation at each, and report whichever layer gives the clearest steering effect for Qwen, not necessarily the passive-best one. GPU 0 only, keep disk usage conservative as in all prior runs (delete large model caches you no longer need). Produce a report stating clearly, with real numbers, whether claims A and B replicate on this different architecture -- explicit side-by-side comparison to the corresponding Pythia-1.4b numbers (probe cosine 0.428, best m=5 rollout cosine 0.637, best steering margin around 0.04) -- and whether this strengthens confidence that the findings are general rather than Pythia-specific.
progress: Cycle 1 review: ACCEPT - The run appears to have executed the intended protocol and met the stated success criteria. The model is explicitly identified as Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B and confirmed base/non-instruct in the required size range. Claim A evidence is complete, with held-out cosine values reported for the best probe, weak baselines, logit-lens/token-identity baselines, and rollout baselines for m={1,3,5,10}. The best probe cosine (0.4284) exceeds all reported weak and token-identity baselines, while rollout baselines at short horizon surpass the probe (already by m=3, and strongly by m=5 and m=10), satisfying the positive replication condition. Claim B evidence is also complete: 5 candidate layers were scanned, each with 5 seeds and norm-relative alpha tuning, and steering margins with 95% CIs were reported. At least one layer—and in fact two layers, 24 and 28—shows a positive steering margin with CI excluding zero, and the best layer’s probe-direction effect greatly exceeds the random-direction control. The final report/artifact list includes the named summaries, CSVs, plots, manifest, report, and inventory. The fact that only 549/600 prompts were usable is a mild deviation from the plan wording, but it was documented transparently and does not invalidate the success criteria as written, which did not require all 600 to remain usable. Overall, this is a successful cross-architecture replication and no further iteration is required.
